newsitem.title: USA: Pill, shots equally effective against Lyme disease.
newsitem.headline: Pill, shots equally effective against Lyme disease.

text.p: Two common treatments for Lyme disease -- one a pill, the other an injection -- are equally effective when signs of the infection have spread beyond the initial site of a tick bite, according to a study in Thursday's New England Journal of Medicine.

The study involved doxycycline, an oral antibiotic sold by many manufacturers, and shots of ceftriaxone, sold under the brand name Rocephin and made by Hoffmann-LaRoche, a subsidiary of Roche Holdings Ltd in Switzerland.
The study at medical centres in New York, Connecticut, Pennsylvania and Wisconsin was supported by a grant from Hoffmann-LaRoche.

Tests were given to 140 volunteers whose Lyme disease had surfaced as neurologic problems, arthritis, or other abnormalities. Dr. Raymond J. Dattwyler of the State University of New York at Stony Brook and his colleagues found that "both treatments were highly effective," failing in only one person in each group.

"This study confirms the current practice of using orally administered doxycycline as a first-line therapy for acute disseminated Lyme disease," the researchers said. The doxycycline treatment is also significantly less expensive.

The initial sign of Lyme disease, believed to be transmitted by ticks, is often a bite mark surrounded by an expanding red ring. That is followed by fever, headache, stiff neck, fatigue or listlessness.
The infection can spread to other tissues. Long-term effects in some people include arthritis, nerve problems, and heart abnormalities.

Usually research on treatments for Lyme disease has lumped together people with all kinds of symptoms. The Dattwyler study was designed to see if patients whose disease had spread should be treated differently from those who simply have the characteristic red ring on their body.
The most common side effect among ceftriaxone recipients was diarrhoea. People treated with doxycycline sometimes reported developing a rash or hypersensitivity to light.
